The Story of Shridatt Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who is the lord of the supreme wealth of omniscience, and I write the story of Shridatt Muni, who endured the suffering inflicted by gods with great peace.

Shridatt was the son of Queen Ela of King Jitshatru of Ilavardhanpuri. He was married to Princess Anshumati, daughter of King Anshuman of Ayodhya. Anshumati had kept a parrot. When the couple played chess, the parrot would mark the score with lines drawn by its claw. But the parrot had a trick: when Shridatt was winning, it drew only one line; when its mistress was winning, it drew two lines. Amazing that even a bird can cheat!

Shridatt tolerated the parrot's trick several times. But finally, he became very angry. He grabbed the parrot by the neck and twisted it. The parrot died instantly. Dying in great anguish, it was reborn as a Vyantar god.

One evening, Shridatt was sitting on his palace roof, watching the beauty of nature. A large cloud passed before his eyes. It had not gone far when, before he could blink, it was torn to pieces. This momentary destruction made a deep impression on Shridatt's mind. All worldly things appeared to him as fleeting as lightning. Sensual pleasures, like venomous serpents, began to frighten him. The body, which he had loved so much, appeared as a repository of all impurity. He realised that those who love this suffering, ever-perishing world and cultivate attachment to it are utterly foolish. He regretted deeply: "Alas, how foolish I have been, not having sought my own welfare until now!" In short, he became deeply detached from the world and ultimately took Jain initiation for the sake of happiness.

Afterward, Monk Shridatt wandered through many lands and cities, awakening many worthy souls and engaging them in self-welfare. While travelling, he once came near his own city. It was winter. One day, Shridatt was standing in kayotsarga meditation outside the city. The Vyantar god — the very parrot whose neck he had twisted — saw him standing in meditation. The god's old enmity arose. He created a terrible storm and began to torment the monk with cold winds and rain. But Shridatt remained unmoved, absorbed in meditation. He endured all the suffering with perfect equanimity.

Seeing the monk's unwavering peace, the Vyantar god was astonished. His enmity melted away. He realised that Shridatt was no longer the man who had killed him — he was a true monk, free from all attachment and aversion. The god bowed to the monk and asked forgiveness. Shridatt blessed him and continued his meditation.

Through dedicated spiritual practice, Shridatt Muni destroyed his karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the consequences of our past actions can be endured with equanimity on the spiritual path. Shridatt's killing of the parrot created a karmic enemy, but through his monastic practice, he was able to endure the resulting suffering without anger or resentment. The wise should understand that all suffering is the fruit of past karma, and by enduring it peacefully, one can exhaust karmic debts and progress toward liberation.
